title: The McCarthy Era's Operative Handed His Playbook to Trump
dek: Roy Cohn was not an aberration of the McCarthy era but a product of the paranoia that seizes American democracy every few decades — and the playbook did not die with him; it carried through to today via Trump.
why: High oral-history density: how Cohn's rules became Trump's rules one by one, with concrete cases and mechanisms, not generalities.
who: Readers and investors interested in the origins of Trump's political style, the history of the McCarthy era, and American political operatics.
skip: The closing Dolly Parton music-review segment is unrelated to this episode's subject and can be skipped.

points.h: Cohn's three rules became Trump's rules
points.body: Bird says Cohn's rules became Trump's rules: never admit error, deny and deny again, and when accused, stall and stall again. That is exactly what Cohn did when he was indicted three times in the 1960s — delay the trial as long as possible, deny the charges, and name and attack the judge. He was a habitual rule-breaker his whole life; rules were for little people, not for him. Trump later copied the playbook wholesale: stiffing people on bills, using delay tactics to cut what he owed to ten cents on the dollar, and paying very little tax through various avoidance schemes.

points.h: He beat the charges on more than tactics — on luck
points.body: Bird and his wife and co-author Susan Goldmark argue in the book that Cohn was partly just lucky. In one trial, a juror's father suddenly died and the judge was forced to declare a mistrial; in another, Cohn's own lawyer suffered a heart attack in court, collapsing just as he was about to give the closing argument. Cohn said on the spot, ‘Judge, I'll do the closing argument myself’, and so got two days, seven hours total, to defend himself — and because he had chosen not to take the witness stand, he was not cross-examined, and the jury acquitted him 12 to 0; some jurors were said to have been moved to tears by him.

points.h: Don't tell me the law, tell me the judge
points.body: Another of Cohn's rules was ‘Don't tell me the law, tell me the judge’ — he knew which judge favored him and which judge could be manipulated. His father, Albert Cohn, was a Bronx judge appointed by the Roosevelt administration, and from childhood he was introduced by his father to lawyers and judges of every kind; after becoming a lawyer at 20, he cultivated judges into friends, highly transactional: do someone a favor first, then knock on the door for the payback. Trump went further on this rule — as president he appointed judges and Supreme Court justices, some of whom later ruled on his own cases. Bird says this is Cohn's most insidious and longest-lasting legacy: he was a lawyer, but he did not care about the law at all; he practiced law by telephone, avoiding leaving any notes or records, and he taught this to Trump.

points.h: In four phone calls, Trump kept praising Cohn
points.body: Bird did four phone interviews with Trump, each about 10 minutes, and they were very strange. The first was a cold call; Trump picked up and said ‘Hello?’, with no idea who Bird was. Bird said he was writing a Cohn biography, and Trump said ‘Oh, great, great, he was a wonderful man, a good lawyer, we won a lot of cases together’, gushing praise for Cohn, genuinely missing him. Bird believes they really were friends. Trump is utterly unashamed of his association with Cohn, which Bird finds baffling — the sordid things in the book are backed by 1,300 footnotes, so how could anyone read it and not feel shame.

Bird says McCarthy was politically an empty shell, not a true ideological believer, who stumbled into this anti-communist witch hunt by accident. But Cohn joined with zeal and professional skill and became McCarthy's brain — McCarthy was by then a functional alcoholic, and Cohn was effectively steering him. They successfully launched a political offensive against the newly installed Eisenhower administration: Cohn was hired in early 1953 and began attacking Eisenhower himself, a Republican president, on the grounds that he was not Republican enough, not anti-communist enough. Cohn was brutal and unrelenting when interrogating witnesses, publicly asking male government employees about their sexual orientation and whether they had had relations with men, destroying the lives of hundreds if not thousands.

Bird says Trump certainly knew Cohn was gay. In the 1970s, after Studio 54 opened in '77, Cohn often took Trump there; in the 1980s Cohn was more open, surrounded at his law firm by a group of young gay men. Once Cohn called Trump to plead for a boyfriend who was dying of AIDS, asking whether he could stay at a Trump hotel; Trump arranged it, the man stayed three or four months, and after he died Trump sent Cohn a bill. Bird sees a connection between Cohn's closeted state and the McCarthy-era persecution of gay people, and Trump's anti-DEI, anti-LGBTQ line today.

points.h: Cohn's politics was the politics of resentment
points.body: Bird traces Cohn's politics in the '60s and '70s: he resented intellectuals, and though a Columbia graduate he hated the Ivy League, preferring to hire young lawyers who had not gone to Ivies; he was suspicious of immigrants, anti-black, an isolationist who wanted America first. He opposed affirmative action, seeing it as discrimination against whites. Bird says this politics is exactly what we see in the Trump administration today, the same politics of resentment. And Trump likewise went to an Ivy, likewise came from a wealthy, high-profile family — the two have a great many parallels.

points.h: The Art of the Deal was arranged by Cohn on his deathbed
points.body: Bird says Cohn did one overlooked thing for Trump: before he died he went to Cy Newhouse, an old classmate from the Horace Mann School and the Condé Nast magazine publisher who also owned Random House, and suggested he have a Random House editor sign Trump to write a memoir. That is where The Art of the Deal came from. The book was published after Cohn's death and became a national bestseller, turning a star developer tucked away in New York into a national figure, a famous businessman, which led to the TV show The Apprentice, which led to Trump running for president. Bird says the starting point of that chain is Cohn's relationship with Cy Newhouse.

points.h: Once Cohn got AIDS, Trump began keeping his distance
points.body: Cohn contracted AIDS early in the epidemic. After Trump learned Cohn might die of AIDS, by all accounts he began keeping his distance, relying less and less on his legal advice and turning to other lawyers, but he never broke with him. Trump also invited Cohn to the newly purchased Florida estate Mar-a-Lago and threw a big dinner, where many people toasted Cohn. After the dinner, Trump is said to have had staff wash the silverware in hydrogen peroxide.

Bird says the core lesson of Cohn's story is this: McCarthyism was not defeated, it did not die, it was not an anomaly of the 1950s. As a historian he came to realize that America is a nation of immigrants, a multicultural nation, a nation with civil liberties and the First Amendment, yet every few decades it goes through a period of paranoia: there was a Red Scare in the 1920s, the McCarthy witch hunt in the early '50s, and now we are in such a period again. In the '50s several thousand civil servants lost their jobs because of Cohn and McCarthy, and today's situation is worse — a more serious attack on democracy, a more serious politics of vengeance, mass hunting down and deportation of undocumented immigrants.
